title: OIDC groups: persist claim and resolve from ACL group: rules
body:
Implements identity-provider groups in the policy — the OIDC `groups` claim → ACL `group:` resolution feature discussed in #1121 and #2366: store the groups the identity provider asserts at login, and let the policy use them. Nothing dynamic: memberships refresh at each login, and `node.expiry` sets how often users log in, as suggested in #2366.

Closes: #2366

## Usage

```yaml
oidc:
  scope: ["openid", "profile", "email", "groups"]
  groups:
    enabled: true          # default false
    domain: example.com    # qualifies every synced group; required when enabled
    # claim: groups        # or cognito:groups, https://example.com/groups, realm_access.roles, …
```

```json
{
  "grants": [
    { "src": ["group:engineering@example.com"], "dst": ["tag:prod"], "ip": ["*"] }
  ]
}
```

`group:<name>@<domain>` is the syntax Tailscale uses for synced groups ([policy syntax](https://tailscale.com/kb/1337/policy-syntax), [Okta](https://tailscale.com/kb/1180/sso-okta-scim), [Entra ID](https://tailscale.com/kb/1249/sso-entra-id-scim)), so policies carry over between Tailscale and Headscale. Synced groups work anywhere a group does: grants, ACLs, SSH rules, `tagOwners` and `autoApprovers`.

## What this changes

- **`groups` and `user_groups` tables** — identity-provider groups and per-user memberships, with explicit SQLite and Postgres DDL created by a migration and by `InitSchema` (no AutoMigrate). Memberships cascade on user and group deletion and carry a `source` (`oidc`), so each source owns its rows: an OIDC login can never clobber memberships a future source (e.g. SCIM) provisions. `source` is deliberately not CHECK-constrained, so adding a source needs no table rebuild.
- **`oidc.groups.enabled`** (default `false`) — opt-in flag. With it off, nothing is stored regardless of what the IdP sends, so the upgrade is a no-op behavior change for existing deployments; turning it off later removes all synced memberships at startup.
- **`oidc.groups.domain`** — qualifies every synced group name, producing the `<name>@<domain>` identifier policies reference. Required when enabled; validated at startup. Changing it removes the previous domain's memberships at startup.
- **`oidc.groups.claim`** (default `"groups"`) — overrides the claim for IdPs that emit memberships under a non-standard key (AWS Cognito's `cognito:groups`, Auth0 namespaced claims, custom `roles`). The literal claim name is tried first (Auth0 URL claims contain dots), then a dotted path into nested claims (Keycloak's `realm_access.roles`). A single string or an array is accepted. Userinfo is preferred over the ID token when it carries the claim, matching how the standard claims are handled. `allowed_groups` is unchanged and keeps reading the standard `groups` claim.
- **Policy resolution (policy v2)** — an undefined `group:<name>@<domain>` resolves to the untagged nodes of users who are members of that synced group. **Synced groups are a separate namespace:** a reference that exactly matches a group defined in the policy's `groups` section is always resolved from its listed members, even if its name contains `@`, so an IdP can never add members to a policy group. That rules out privilege escalation by naming an IdP group after a policy group used for `tagOwners` or `autoApprovers`. Undefined plain `group:x` is still a validation error (typos are still caught); a synced group nobody belongs to is valid and grants nothing, failing closed as in Tailscale.
- **Revocation** — each login *replaces* the user's OIDC memberships. A group removed at the IdP, or a login without a groups claim, removes the membership; a login that authenticates but is rejected by authorization (e.g. no longer in `allowed_groups`) removes all of them. `User.PolicyEqual` includes group names, so the policy recompiles when memberships change, and only then.
- **Propagation** — a membership change is broadcast from the OIDC callback so already-connected peers get updated filters immediately, without a restart. Only that policy delta is sent, and only when memberships actually changed. The login's user change itself stays unbroadcast, as upstream fixed in #2890, so a new node's registration still announces the node and #2888 cannot come back. The broadcast is needed here because the registration or SSH check that follows finds the policy manager already updated, and because a user who abandons the flow must still lose revoked groups.
- **Visibility** — `groups` is returned in the v1 `User` response (always an array; generated client and recorded v1 responses updated) and shown as a Groups column in `headscale users list`. The NodeStore's copies of a user are refreshed when their groups change, so node responses show current groups too.

Fixes along the way, each of which this feature depends on:

- **Parser order.** The alias, owner and auto-approver parsers checked the username `@` heuristic before the `group:` prefix, so any group reference containing `@` was silently parsed as a username that matched no one.
- **Per-node grants.** A user change that only affected per-node grants (`via`, `autogroup:self`) — e.g. a rename — never cleared the per-node filter caches or reported a policy change, so those nodes kept stale filters and nothing was broadcast. Group memberships would make this the normal path for granting and revoking access, so the compiled grants are now part of change detection. Separate commit.

## Security and robustness

- **Case folding** — only ASCII letters are folded, identically on ingest and in policy references, so Unicode lookalikes (e.g. the Kelvin sign `K` vs `k`) cannot resolve to another group.
- **Names** — lowercased and trimmed; a name the IdP already sends qualified with the configured domain (providers that name groups by email address) is accepted as is; other names containing `@` are ignored with a warning since they cannot be referenced unambiguously.
- **Stale writes** — the `User.Memberships` association is read-only in gorm, so saving a stale in-memory user can never write revoked memberships back (covered by a test).
- **Concurrency** — on Postgres, concurrent syncs for the same user are serialised with a row lock, so two simultaneous logins replace rather than merge each other's sets. Membership comparison uses Go byte order rather than the database collation.
- **Performance** — memberships are preloaded with users in a fixed number of queries; the policy manager never touches the database during compilation. Membership checks are in memory and allocation-free: ~3 ms per group reference at 5,000 users × 100 groups each (benchmark included).

## Vendor neutrality

The implementation is intentionally vendor-agnostic — memberships are plain strings and resolution is exact matching of qualified names. It works against the standard OIDC `groups` claim shape (Authelia, Authentik, Keycloak, Okta with the groups scope, Google Workspace via Dex, Entra ID via app-role or group-ID claims — `group:<object-id>@<domain>` works as in Tailscale) and against the custom-claim path (AWS Cognito, Auth0 namespaced claims, custom `roles`-style claims, and nested claims such as Keycloak's `realm_access.roles`).

## Tests

- **DB** — set/replace/clear, per-source isolation, preloading, the read-only association (a stale `User` save can't re-grant a revoked group), cascade on user delete, and prune — each on SQLite **and Postgres**. The existing migration and schema validation runs over every test dump with the new migration.
- **Policy** — resolution, ASCII-only case-insensitivity, fail-closed, namespace separation (policy groups with and without `@`), validation in ACLs, SSH, `tagOwners` and `autoApprovers`, recompile on gain and loss, per-node grants (`via`, `autogroup:self`, rename) checked against a freshly compiled policy, tag ownership read from current users, and a parser regression test.
- **OIDC** — real logins through the callback against `mockoidc`: sync, normalisation, qualification, revocation at the next login, revocation on a rejected login, feature off, and userinfo-vs-ID-token precedence.
- **State** — startup prune on disable and on domain change; a change is reported only when memberships change; node copies of the user are refreshed.
- **Config and API** — validation and loading of `oidc.groups.*`; v1 `groups` field populated.
- **Integration** — two mockoidc-driven end-to-end tests in `integration/auth_oidc_groups_test.go`, added to the generated CI matrix:
  - `TestOIDCGroupsGrantAndRevokeAccess` connects an anchor peer and logs the OIDC user in three times (no groups → member of `Engineering` → no groups) under an ACL written as `group:engineering@example.com`. It asserts through the anchor's `PacketFilter` that the grant arrives without a server restart and is revoked when the IdP drops the group.
  - `TestOIDCGroupsDisabledDoesNotPersist` checks that nothing is stored with sync off, the default.

  No external IdP or third-party service is required at CI time. This addresses the maintenance concern raised in #1121 ("we are actively avoiding platforms we cannot have full end-to-end tests as it is unfeasible for us to maintain it over time").
- `golangci-lint` reports no issues on the new code, `mkdocs build --strict` passes, and every commit builds on its own.

## Notes for review

- **Commits** are split by layer (types → db → policy → per-node fix → oidc → api → integration → docs) so each can be reviewed and bisected on its own.
- **Refresh model is snapshot-on-login.** Groups update when the user re-authenticates against the IdP, not on a timer. `node.expiry` sets how often users re-authenticate, and so how often memberships refresh; memberships apply to all of a user's nodes between logins. This is the "nothing dynamic, nothing fancy" model called for in #1121 and matches the acceptable trade-off kradalby outlined in #2366. Other refresh mechanisms discussed in the issue threads (offline-access + UserInfo polling, LDAP federation, SCIM v2 provisioning) all still need a place to persist the IdP's group memberships for policy evaluation. They would build on the per-source `user_groups` storage and the change propagation this PR introduces, not replace it — SCIM, for example, becomes a `scim` source without changing how the policy resolves groups. Those approaches are out of scope here per kradalby's prior call. If there is appetite for any of these (SCIM v2, LDAP, etc.) I'd be happy to work on them in separate PRs.
- **Production validation and maintenance commitment.** I'm running this fork today across multiple environments — Dex + Google Workspace and Microsoft Entra ID as the IdPs, Headplane, SQLite, Kubernetes — where OIDC group resolution was a hard requirement for the deployments. I've deployed headscale in many environments over time; since I had to do this work anyway, contributing it upstream felt like the right way to give back. I'm a big fan of the project and the maintainers' work, committed to maintaining this feature long term, and fully open to discussion or refactors that come out of review.

Refs: #1121, #2366

`gh api --paginate` already concatenates pages into one JSON array, so `from json` yields a list of records directly. Drop both `| flatten` calls.

title: policy/v2: fix empty grants/acls returning FilterAllowAll
body:
`compileFilterRules`, `compileGrants`, and `updateLocked` guarded their "no rules so allow all" fallback with `len(pol.Grants) == 0`, which matches both an absent `grants` field and an explicit empty array. JSON `{"grants": []}` unmarshals to a non-nil empty slice and should compile to zero filter rules (deny all) to match Tailscale SaaS, but the length check sent it down the `FilterAllowAll` path.

Switch the guard to `pol.Grants == nil`, the same nil-vs-empty asymmetry already used for `ACLs`. `{}` keeps allowing all; `{"acls": []}` and `{"grants": []}` now both deny all.

Fixes #3211

title: .github: gate PRs via mitchellh/vouch
body:
PRs keep arriving without the prior discussion `CONTRIBUTING.md` asks
for. We are not able to review or triage PRs fast enough, specially now that everyone has super human code generation capabilities.

Adopt [mitchellh/vouch](https://github.com/mitchellh/vouch) to
auto-close PRs from authors not on `.github/VOUCHED.td`. Issues stay
open to everyone — the close message points contributors back at
`CONTRIBUTING.md` to start that discussion.

Less aggressive than ghostty, which gates issues too.

Seed list is past PR contributors with merged code plus authors of
detailed issues; bots and CODEOWNERS are auto-vouched. Anyone with an
open PR that hasn't been through review yet was left off — `!vouch`

title: policy: surface exit nodes via autogroup:internet

`compileFilterRules` skipped `autogroup:internet` destinations to keep them out of the wire-format `PacketFilter`, but those compiled rules also feed `pm.matchers`. `Node.CanAccess` looks at a matcher whose `DestsIsTheInternet` covers the public internet to surface exit-node peers to ACL sources — with the skip in place no such matcher existed, exit nodes silently dropped out of the source's peer list, and the `ref/routes/#setup-an-exit-node` walkthrough stopped working: `tailscale exit-node list` returned `no exit nodes found` and `tailscale set --exit-node=<ip>` returned `no node found in netmap with IP`.

The skip lands in `filter.go`. Removing it lets `autogroup:internet` flow through normal matcher derivation. To keep the wire-format PacketFilter correct on advertisers, `ReduceFilterRules` now keeps a destination on exit-route advertisers when every prefix sits inside `util.TheInternet()` — Tailscale SaaS sends those rules to exit nodes so the advertiser's kernel filter accepts traffic forwarded by `autogroup:internet` sources.

title: state: fix HA tracking losing secondary after all routers offline
body:
When all subnet routers serving a prefix go offline simultaneously and one returns, headscale could end up with the returning node marked online in `NodeStore` but absent from `PrimaryRoutes` for the prefix, with HA tracking stuck until daemon restart.

The generation counter added in b09af384 closed the obvious window but left the gen check non-atomic with the subsequent `NodeStore.UpdateNode` and `PrimaryRoutes.SetRoutes` calls. A concurrent `Connect` that bumped the counter and rewrote primary routes could be silently overtaken by a stale `Disconnect`'s `SetRoutes(empty)`. The grace-period flow in `poll.go` hides this on most cable-pull cadences, which is why three earlier reproductions (servertest graceful, integration graceful, integration cable-pull-via-iptables) all pass on main.

Replace the standalone counter with a per-node `nodeLock` pairing the gen counter and a mutex. `Connect` and `Disconnect` now run under the lock and re-check gen inside the critical section, making gen evaluation and the mutations atomic. Per-node so unrelated nodes never contend; same-node steady state has effectively no contention.

`TestConnectDisconnectRace` drives the race directly through `State`, fails deterministically on main, and passes under the lock. The earlier servertest, integration and cable-pull reproductions stay as regression coverage for the user-reported sequence. A property test on `PrimaryRoutes` joins as a safety net for future changes to primary route selection.

Fixes #3203

title: ci: fetch full history in lint workflow for --new-from-rev
body:
- [x] have read the [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md) file
- [ ] raised a GitHub issue or discussed it on the projects chat beforehand
- [ ] added unit tests
- [ ] added integration tests
- [ ] updated documentation if needed

The `golangci-lint` job in `.github/workflows/lint.yml` runs with `--new-from-rev=${{ github.event.pull_request.base.sha }}` to filter reported issues to lines added by the PR. The checkout step uses `fetch-depth: 2`, which is only enough for single-commit PRs. For PRs with N > 1 commits, base.sha lives at HEAD~N and is not in the fetched history, so revgrep fails:

```
fatal: bad object <base-sha>
[runner] Can't process results by diff processor
```

When the diff processor fails open, golangci-lint reports every existing issue in the repo, drowning out anything actually new in the PR and forcing maintainers to ignore the check.

Reproduction:

```
git clone --depth 2 --branch <multi-commit-pr-branch> ...
cd ...
git cat-file -e <base-sha>; echo $?  # => 1
```

Fix: `fetch-depth: 0` (full history). Matches the pattern already in `release.yml:18` and `docs-deploy.yml:26`. Only the `golangci-lint` job changes; `prettier-lint` and `proto-lint` do not use `--new-from-rev`.

title: hscontrol/policy: reject ambiguous user references at policy load

title: cmd/vendorhash: track vendor SRI in flakehashes.json
body:
Replaces the manual `flake.nix` vendor hash literal with a content-
addressed `flakehashes.json` file maintained by a small Go tool that
imports `tailscale.com/cmd/nardump/nardump.SRI` directly. Schema and
fingerprint algorithm mirror upstream's `tool/updateflakes` from
[tailscale/tailscale#19551](https://github.com/tailscale/tailscale/pull/19551)
so a future shared library extraction is trivial.

Today the hash lives as a string in `flake.nix:30` and the only
divergence detector is the CI step that scrapes `specified:` /
`got:` lines from `nix build` stderr. The round-trip is push → wait
for CI → read PR comment → paste new hash. Brittle and slow.

`vendorhash check` does a sha256 over `go.mod` and `go.sum`. If the
fingerprint matches `flakehashes.json`, exit silently. Only an actual
drift triggers `go mod vendor` + `nardump.SRI`. That makes the new
prek hook cheap enough to run on every commit touching `go.mod`,
catching staleness locally instead of at CI time. CI itself now runs
the same tool and reads structured output, dropping the grep/awk.

Pulls in `tailscale.com v1.97.0-pre.0.20260429005429-40088602c960`
to get the nardump library split (post-`v1.96.4`); cascades into a
go directive bump to `1.26.2` and a nixpkgs lock advance for the

title: policy/v2: add support for policy tests
body:
Tailscale policies have a `tests` block where the operator says, for a given source, what should be reachable. v2 ignored it — a policy whose tests contradicted its own ACLs would still apply.

`SetPolicy` now compiles the new policy in a sandbox, runs the tests, and rejects on failure without touching the live `PolicyManager`. `NewPolicyManager` skips evaluation so a stale stored policy whose referenced user was deleted does not block boot. `headscale policy check` opens the database under `--bypass-grpc-and-access-database-directly` (same flag `set` and `get` already accept) and runs tests against live data.

Error messages match Tailscale SaaS so policies move between control planes without rewriting. Comparing against captured SaaS responses surfaced two engine bugs. `Protocol.UnmarshalJSON` stored whichever form the user wrote, so `proto: "6", dst: "host:443"` was rejected at parse though SaaS accepts it — `UnmarshalJSON` now canonicalises numeric IANA forms to the name. `srcReachesDst` passed empty Protocol through to `ruleMatchesProto`, which short-circuited any rule with an `IPProto` restriction, so a TCP-only grant could not satisfy a default-proto test — empty Protocol now expands to `{TCP, UDP, ICMP, ICMPv6}` at the call site.

Parse-time schema validation rejects test shapes SaaS rejects: single-port dst, proto in `{tcp, udp, sctp, ""}`, no `autogroup:internet` dst, no CIDR-typed dst, at least one of `accept`/`deny`.

Closes #3005

title: oidc: handle groups claim as string or array (FlexibleStringSlice)
body:
Some OIDC providers (notably JumpCloud) return the `groups` claim as a plain string when the user belongs to a single group, rather than a single-element array:

title: integration: retry transient docker network ops
body:
`TestHASubnetRouterFailoverDockerDisconnect` flaked on phase 4c reconnect (5/6 attempts on [#3226](https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/pull/3226) CI). Debugging surfaced three independent bugs:

**Docker daemon eventual-consistency on connect.** `ConnectNetwork` right after a matching `DisconnectNetwork` returns transient errors like `endpoint with name X already exists`. `dockertestutil` now wraps the daemon calls in `backoff.Retry` with 30s `MaxElapsedTime`.

**Force-disconnect leaks routes.** `DisconnectNetwork(Force=true)` left stale entries in the container's namespace route table; the next `ConnectNetwork` failed with `cannot program address ... conflicts with existing route` and never recovered on its own, so the retry above exhausted instead of absorbing. Drop `Force`. Cable-pull semantic preserved — paired probe timeouts on both routers are visible in prober logs while they are physically disconnected.

**HA prober deadlocks when two or more nodes time out in one cycle.** `time.After(ProbeTimeout)` returned a single channel shared by every probe goroutine. The first goroutine to receive drains it; others park on `responseCh` forever, `wg.Wait()` never returns, the scheduler loop in `app.go` stops ticking. Per-goroutine timer fixes it.

Plus: `gh-action-integration-generator.go` no longer recurses into `integration/` subpackages, so the new `dockertestutil` unit tests stay as plain `go test` jobs rather than being promoted to Docker-based integration matrix entries.

Three consecutive local runs of the test pass cleanly. Unit tests for `retryDockerOp` lock recovery and context-bound behaviour.

title: [Feature] Tailscale SaaS-like regional subnet routing

### Use case

Regional Routing for subnet routers: https://tailscale.com/blog/regional-routing

Given that [custom DERPs cannot be used in regional routing even with SaaS](https://github.com/tailscale/tailscale/issues/12993), we might fall back to using DERP IDs -- for each client, we should make its preferred subnet router to be the one it's sharing the same DERP with (if any), and fall back to the lowest Node ID selection if needed.

- [x] I can contribute this feature

When clients need AllowedIPs for a prefix, instead of blindly picking the node with lowest NodeID to use as subnet router, pick up the subnet router sharing the same DERP ID.

title: policy/v2: fix autogroup:internet via grants on exit nodes
body:
A grant of the form `{src: alice, dst: autogroup:internet, via: tag:exit1}` was loading without error but stripping every exit node from alice's view — `tailscale exit-node list` returned "no exit nodes found".

Two sites in `policy/v2` skipped `autogroup:internet` at the compile / steering layer: `compileViaForNode`'s `*AutoGroup` arm produced no `FilterRule` for the via-tagged exit node, and `ViaRoutesForPeer`'s `*AutoGroup` arm produced no `Include`/`Exclude`. With `pm.needsPerNodeFilter` true, the exit node's matchers were empty, `BuildPeerMap` could not link source to exit, and `RoutesForPeer`'s `ReduceRoutes` stripped `0.0.0.0/0` and `::/0` from `AllowedIPs`.

The skip belongs at the wire-format layer (`ReduceFilterRules`), not at the compile layer that also feeds internal matchers. This PR lifts `autogroup:internet` handling into both `*AutoGroup` arms with the same shape used for `*Prefix` destinations: emit a `TheInternet` rule on via-tagged exit advertisers; surface `peer.ExitRoutes()` in `Include` when the peer carries the via tag, `Exclude` otherwise. `ReduceFilterRules` continues to keep the rule on exit-route advertisers' wire output and strip it elsewhere, preserving the SaaS PacketFilter encoding.

Reproduction lives in `hscontrol/policy/v2/issue_3233_test.go` (unit) and `TestGrantViaExitNodeInternetVisibility` in `hscontrol/servertest/grants_test.go` (end-to-end via netmap).

Sibling testdata directories are already case-clean: `acl_results/` uses lowercase only, `routes_results/` uses lowercase only, `grant_results/` uses lowercase only. `ssh_results/` is the only one carrying both cases.

**Impact on macOS contributors:** APFS is case-insensitive by default, so only one of `SSH-A1.hujson`/`ssh-a1.hujson` can physically exist on disk after checkout. Whichever the OS keeps, the other shows up as "modified" in `git status`, producing a permanent dirty submodule state for downstream consumers.

**Proposed fix:** delete the uppercase `SSH-*.hujson` files. They appear to be a leftover from the pre-`tscap` era of SSH compat testing.

Happy to send a PR if this is the right call.

title: panic: nil pointer in HandleNodeFromPreAuthKey when re-registering a tagged node under a different user (noise control plane; sibling of #3038 / PR #3046, unfixed in this path)
body:
## Summary

`HandleNodeFromPreAuthKey` at `hscontrol/state/state.go:1894` calls `oldUser.Name()` on a `UserView` whose backing `*User` pointer is `nil`, panicking with `runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference` at `hscontrol/types/types_view.go:97`.

This is the **same nil-deref class** that PR #3046 (merged 2026-02-04 → v0.28.0) fixed in `HandleNodeFromAuthPath` (gRPC `RegisterNode`). The patch was scoped to a single callsite, leaving the parallel noise-control-plane entry point unguarded.

## Affected code path (v0.28.0, commit 97fa117c)

`hscontrol/state/state.go:1880–1899` — the "Node exists but belongs to a different user" branch:

```go
existingNodeAnyUser, existsAnyUser := s.nodeStore.GetNodeByMachineKeyAnyUser(machineKey)
if pak.User != nil && existsAnyUser && existingNodeAnyUser.Valid() && existingNodeAnyUser.UserID().Get() != pak.User.ID {
    oldUser := existingNodeAnyUser.User()             // returns UserView{ж: <*User from nodeStore>}
    log.Info().
        ...
        Str("old.user", oldUser.Name()).               // panics here when oldUser.ж is nil
        ...
        Msg("Creating new node for different user (same machine key exists for another user)")
}
```

`NodeView.User()` is a thin wrapper that returns `v.ж.User.View()` (`hscontrol/types/types_view.go:224`). When the cached node's `User *User` is `nil` (because the node was loaded with a `Preload("User")` whose joined `users` row didn't exist), `.View()` produces a `UserView{ж: nil}`, and `UserView.Name()` (line 97) does `return v.ж.Name` — nil deref.

## Versions

- Headscale `v0.28.0` commit `97fa117c48a58bee3941e5e8b4393873501afe14`
- Tailscale client `1.96.4`
- Database: SQLite (default)
- Container/proxy: tested both with and without (Caddy reverse proxy in production, bare HTTP in reproducer)

## How this differs from the production trigger path

Important context up front, so reviewers can calibrate the reproducer:

- **What we observed in production:** an existing tagged subnet-router node, registered via a `tag:subnet-router` preauthkey under a real user, hit this panic when its containerized `tailscaled` was restarted and presented a *new* preauthkey bound to a *different* real user. The orphan-user-pointer state in `nodeStore` was already present — it appeared to have been seeded at runtime via Headscale's tags-as-identity / tagged-devices conversion machinery (closely related to #3161, which describes the same data-corruption class on the UI/CLI listing path).
- **What the reproducer does:** short-circuits the *creation* of that orphan state by using SQLite schema surgery (drop the `fk_nodes_user` constraint, set `node.user_id` to a non-existent `users.id`, restart). This is **not** how production reached the state — it's the cheapest way to get the same in-memory shape (`Node.User == nil`) past Headscale's startup FK validation so the buggy code path can be exercised deterministically.
- **Why this is still load-bearing evidence:** the panic is a property of the `oldUser.Name()` call inside `HandleNodeFromPreAuthKey`. Whatever the upstream cause of the nil-backed `UserView`, the panic site is the same single line. The reproducer demonstrates that the post-PR-#3046 v0.28.0 code path is unguarded in this function — independently of which production code path manufactured the orphan state.

If maintainers want a reproducer that arrives at the orphan state via the same upstream path as production rather than via schema surgery, that would require working back through the tagged-devices conversion logic; happy to expand if useful, but the panic-site fix is independent of that investigation.

## Reproducer

Self-contained, ~2 minutes to set up. Note: the schema-surgery step is a deliberate shortcut — see "How this differs from the production trigger path" above for context.

```bash
EOF

{"acls":[{"action":"accept","src":["*"],"dst":["*:*"]}]}
EOF

bin/headscale -c etc/config.yaml serve > logs/hs.log 2>&1 &

# 2. Register a node under a real user (any tailscaled instance works here)
bin/headscale -c etc/config.yaml users create userA

# ... point a tailscaled at http://127.0.0.1:8081 with $KEY ...
# (one node row at id=1 with user_id=1 will be created)

# 3. Stop headscale, surgically remove the FK constraint on nodes.user_id,
#    orphan the node row, restart.
pkill -f bin/headscale
python3 <<'PYEOF'
import sqlite3
c = sqlite3.connect("/tmp/hs/data/db.sqlite"); cur = c.cursor()
cur.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys = OFF")
cur.execute("ALTER TABLE nodes RENAME TO nodes_old")
# Recreate without `fk_nodes_user`:

  id integer PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, machine_key text, node_key text, disco_key text,

  created_at datetime, updated_at datetime, deleted_at datetime)""")
cur.execute("INSERT INTO nodes SELECT * FROM nodes_old"); cur.execute("DROP TABLE nodes_old")
cur.execute("UPDATE nodes SET user_id = 99999999 WHERE id = 1")  # any non-existent users.id
c.commit()
PYEOF
bin/headscale -c etc/config.yaml serve > logs/hs.log 2>&1 &

# 4. Mint a preauthkey under a *different* real user, force tailscaled to reauth
bin/headscale -c etc/config.yaml users create userB
```

```
	/home/runner/work/headscale/headscale/hscontrol/noise.go:257

	/home/runner/work/headscale/headscale/hscontrol/noise.go:271 +0x27e
net/http.HandlerFunc.ServeHTTP(...)
	/nix/store/.../net/http/server.go:2322 +0x29

	/home/runner/work/headscale/headscale/hscontrol/metrics.go:74 +0x26c
github.com/gorilla/mux.(*Router).ServeHTTP(...)

created by golang.org/x/net/http2.(*serverConn).scheduleHandler in goroutine 63
```

## Trace context (lines preceding the panic)

```
2026-04-30T23:33:50-04:00 TRC hscontrol/noise.go:54 > Noise upgrade handler for client 127.0.0.1:39408
2026-04-30T23:33:50-04:00 DBG hscontrol/types/preauth_key.go:124 > PreAuthKey.Validate: checking key expiration=... reusable=true used=false
2026-04-30T23:33:50-04:00 DBG hscontrol/state/state.go:1790 > Registering node with pre-auth key machine.key=[KOgA8] node.key=[GTFSB] node.name=repro-node user.name=userB
2026/04/30 23:33:50 http2: panic serving 127.0.0.1:39408: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
```

The panic fires at the `log.Info().Str("old.user", oldUser.Name())` call inside the "different user" branch. The http2 server's deferred `runHandler.func1` recovers the panic, so the headscale process **does not exit** — but the registration is never completed. A retrying client produces a panic per attempt; in our production incident this manifested as **1,902 panics in one hour** during a `tailscaled` reconnection loop.

## Why PR #3046 didn't catch this

[PR #3046](https://github.com/juanfont/headscale/pull/3046) fixed the equivalent nil-deref in `HandleNodeFromAuthPath` (gRPC entry, used by web/CLI registration flows). The diff is scoped to:

```
@@ -1368,140 +1557,75 @@ func (s *State) HandleNodeFromAuthPath(
```

`HandleNodeFromPreAuthKey` (noise control plane entry, used by all `tailscaled` clients on `tailscale up --authkey=...`) lives in the same file but in a **separate function** (line ~1670 onward in v0.28.0). PR #3046's diff context lines confirm `HandleNodeFromPreAuthKey` was untouched.

## Suggested fix

Mirror the guard pattern from PR #3046. Either:

1. Nil-check the result of `existingNodeAnyUser.User()` before calling `.Name()`:
    ```go
    oldUser := existingNodeAnyUser.User()
    oldUserName := "<unknown>"
    if oldUser.Valid() {
        oldUserName = oldUser.Name()
    }
    log.Info().Caller().Str("old.user", oldUserName)...
    ```
2. Or fix at the source — make `nodeStore.GetNodeByMachineKeyAnyUser` populate the `User` field defensively (e.g., fall back to a synthetic `<deleted user N>` UserView when the join misses), so all callers are protected.

Option 2 is more durable; option 1 is a minimal targeted patch matching the existing fix shape.

## Notes / pre-empting Debug-info gap

- **Trace log**: included above for the reproducer. Production trace is not available because Headscale wasn't running with `log.level: trace` at incident time, and re-triggering on production would require resurrecting the orphan-user state.
- **Client netmap**: structurally not capturable for this bug — registration aborts inside the noise handler before the client reaches the netmap stage. The reproducer's `tailscaled` log shows the same: `tailscale up` hangs awaiting an HTTP/2 response that never arrives.
- **Reproducer fidelity**: see "How this differs from the production trigger path" above — the schema-surgery shortcut is intentional and bounded to the panic-site demonstration.

title: IPAllocator uses monotonic counter — deleted node IPs not recycled, risk of IPv4 pool exhaustion
body:
## Summary

When a node is deleted, its IP address is **not returned to the free pool**. The `IPAllocator` uses a monotonic counter that only increments, never recycles. Over time this will exhaust the available `/100.64.0.0/10` CGNAT range (~4 million IPs), making it impossible to register new nodes.

## Affected Version

Headscale v0.28.0

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Register many nodes (or repeatedly register & delete the same node)
2. Observe that each new node receives the *next* IP in sequence rather than a previously-freed one
3. Eventually `IPAllocator.next()` exhausts the available range

## Root Cause

`hscontrol/db/ip.go` — `IPAllocator.next()` works with a monotonic counter:

```go
// Simplified pseudocode:
func (i *IPAllocator) next(...) (netip.Addr, error) {
    last := i.lastIPs[prefix]
    next := last.Next()           // always increments, never checks free list
    i.lastIPs[prefix] = next
    return next, nil
}
```

When a node is deleted via `DeleteNode`, its IP is removed from the DB but **not added back** to a free list. The allocator has no concept of "previously used, now available again" addresses.

## Impact

- **Production risk**: Networks with many ephemeral nodes (CI runners, test devices, repeated re-registrations) will eventually exhaust the pool.
- **CGNAT /100.64.0.0/10** has ~4,194,304 addresses — large but finite.
- **No self-healing**: Once exhausted, no new nodes can be registered without a manual DB repair.

## Proposed Fix

Add a **free-list** (or bitmap) approach:

1. On `DeleteNode`: add the freed IP(s) to an in-memory free-list (protected by mutex)
2. In `IPAllocator.next()`: check the free-list first before incrementing the counter
3. Persist the free-list to the database so it survives restarts

```go
type IPAllocator struct {
    mu       sync.Mutex
    freeList map[netip.Prefix][]netip.Addr  // recycled IPs
    lastIPs  map[netip.Prefix]netip.Addr
}

func (i *IPAllocator) Release(prefix netip.Prefix, addr netip.Addr) {
    i.mu.Lock()
    defer i.mu.Unlock()
    i.freeList[prefix] = append(i.freeList[prefix], addr)
}

func (i *IPAllocator) next(prefix netip.Prefix) (netip.Addr, error) {
    i.mu.Lock()
    defer i.mu.Unlock()
    if len(i.freeList[prefix]) > 0 {
        // Reuse a freed IP
        addr := i.freeList[prefix][0]
        i.freeList[prefix] = i.freeList[prefix][1:]
        return addr, nil
    }
    // Fall back to monotonic increment
    last := i.lastIPs[prefix]
    next := last.Next()
    i.lastIPs[prefix] = next
    return next, nil
}
```

Alternatively, a **bitmap** over the address range would be more memory-efficient for large deployments.

## Additional Context

- This was noticed while operating a self-hosted Headscale instance with multiple worker nodes that are occasionally re-registered
- The current behaviour is surprising: users expect that deleting a node frees its address for future reuse
- Related: if the DB is clean-wiped and rebuilt, `lastIPs` should be recalculated from the *maximum* currently-allocated IP, not zero (otherwise collisions are possible)

## Checklist

- [x] I have searched existing issues and this is not a duplicate
- [x] I can reproduce this on v0.28.0
- [x] I am running a self-hosted instance (not Tailscale SaaS)

title: policy: implement nodeAttrs support
body:
Closes #2319

This PR adds support for `nodeAttrs` in the Tailscale ACL policy, allowing operators to attach arbitrary capabilities to nodes via the policy file. These capabilities are distributed to clients through the CapMap field in MapResponse, enabling Tailscale client-side features that depend on node attributes.

## What is implemented

- **HuJSON parsing**: `nodeAttrs` array is parsed from the policy file alongside existing `acls` and `grants`.
- **Target matching**: Supports user emails, tags (`tag:server`), IP addresses (IPv4/IPv6), and wildcard (`*`).
- **Tag ownership semantics**: Respects the existing "tags XOR user ownership" rule—tagged nodes are owned by `TaggedDevices`, not the creating user.
- **CapMap distribution**: Compiled `NodeCapMap` is included in `MapResponse` for all affected nodes on policy changes.
- **Self-node invalidation**: When a policy change affects nodeAttrs, the mapper correctly invalidates the self node so clients receive updated CapMap without reconnecting.

## Test coverage

- `hscontrol/policy/v2/nodeattrs_test.go`: Unit tests for all target types (user, tag, IP, wildcard) and multiple-grant merge semantics.
- `hscontrol/servertest/nodeattrs_test.go`: End-to-end server-level tests verifying CapMap appears in Netmap after policy reload.
- `integration/nodeattrs_test.go`: Docker-based E2E tests verifying real tailscale clients receive and apply nodeAttrs dynamically.
- `BenchmarkCompileNodeAttrs`: Micro-benchmark for regression tracking of CapMap compilation cost.

## Compatibility

- Old clients (CapVer < 81) ignore CapMap; behavior is unchanged.
- Policies without `nodeAttrs` behave exactly as before.
- No database migration required.

## Future work (out of scope)

Some nodeAttrs require server-side features beyond CapMap distribution (e.g., `ippool` in #2912). This PR only covers the "string-only" CapMap path.

 ### Summary                                                                                                                                                                                                                  
   
  `policyChangeResponse` sends `PeersChanged` for current peers but never calls `WithUserProfiles(currentPeers)`. When a policy change fires alongside a new cross-user peer joining (i.e. user list grows), the resulting     
  `MapResponse` carries the new peer in `PeersChanged` but no entry in `UserProfiles` for that peer's owner. On the client, `mapSession.addUserProfile` silently skips users it has never seen in `lastUserProfile`, so the
  netmap ends up with `len(Peers) == n` but `nm.UserProfiles[peer.User()]` missing.                                                                                                                                            
                                                         
  The non-policy path (`buildFromChange`, `mapper.go:298`) already does this correctly:                                                                                                                                        
   
  ```go                                                                                                                                                                                                                        
  if len(resp.PeersChanged) > 0 {                        
      peers := m.state.ListPeers(nodeID, resp.PeersChanged...)
      builder.WithUserProfiles(peers)   // ← present
      builder.WithPeerChanges(peers)                                                                                                                                                                                           
  }
  ```                                                                                                                                                                                                                          
                                                         
  `policyChangeResponse` is missing the same call.

  ### Reproducer                                                                                                                                                                                                               
   
 This PR adds `TestIssuesMapContent/policy_change_carries_user_profile_for_new_peer` in `hscontrol/servertest/issues_test.go`, which deterministically exercises the buggy path by inserting `node2` straight into `NodeStore` and firing an explicit `change.PolicyChange()`. This test guarantees that `c1`'s first view of the peer arrives via `policyChangeResponse` — independent of registration      
  timing.                                                
                                                                                                                                                                                                                               
  The same bug also surfaces in the existing `TestIssuesMapContent/all_peers_have_user_profiles`, but only as a flaky failure: when registration is fast, the per-peer `NodeAdded` change wins the race against the user-list  
  policy change and delivers `UserProfiles[user2]` via `buildFromChange`. When registration is even ~1–2s slower, the policy-change update lands first or
  coalesces with the peer-added one inside `policyChangeResponse`, and the profile is dropped.                                                                                                                                 
                                                         
  The bug is latent in `master` — it surfaces deterministically as soon as anything stretches registration timing.

title: policy: implement nodeAttrs

Two unrelated build/CI fixes split out of #3251.

**Dockerfile.tailscale-HEAD, Dockerfile.derper: bump golang to 1.26.3**

Tailscale upstream `go.mod` now requires 1.26.3. Headscale's tailscale-HEAD and DERPer builder images still pin 1.26.2, so the HEAD build fails on the toolchain check.

**ci: fetch full history in golangci-lint job**

`revgrep` needs `pull_request.base.sha` reachable in the local clone to compute the diff against new code. With `fetch-depth: 2` only HEAD and one parent are fetched, so a stale base SHA (when main moves between PR syncs) is not reachable, revgrep falls through, and pre-existing issues outside the PR scope get surfaced as lint failures.

title: policy/matcher: include CapGrant.Dsts in match destinations
body:
`MatchFromFilterRule` derives a node's `Match` from its `tailcfg.FilterRule`, but only read `DstPorts[].IP`. Cap-grant-only rules (`tailscale.com/cap/relay` and friends) carry their destinations in `CapGrant[].Dsts`, so the matcher's dest IPSet was empty, `BuildPeerMap` / `ReduceNodes` never crossed the source ↔ cap-target relationship, and the relay node stayed invisible. Clients then never attempted peer-relay paths and connections sat on DERP.

Union `CapGrant[].Dsts` into the dest IPSet alongside `DstPorts`. One narrow site, the exact location of the wrong invariant — not a symptom-level workaround in the policy compiler or peer-map builder. Restores visibility for every cap-grant-only relationship, with peer relay the most visible instance.

Coverage: `MatchFromFilterRule` unit cases for cap-grant-only, companion-cap, and mixed `DstPorts`+`CapGrant` rules; an end-to-end `BuildPeerMap` regression across every alias form documented at https://tailscale.com/docs/features/peer-relay — `hosts` block + `autogroup:member`, `tag:X` → `tag:Y`, tag → raw Tailscale IP, and user-email → hostname.

Fixes #3256

title: panic: nil State in LockFreeBatcher worker during startup connect storm (v0.28.0)
body:
## Summary

`v0.28.0` Headscale panicked with a nil-pointer dereference in `state.(*State).ListPeers` ~5s after a systemd restart, while ~250 nodes were reconnecting. The crash originates from a `LockFreeBatcher` worker servicing a node change event before the mapper's `State` reference is wired.

## Version

```
headscale version v0.28.0
commit: 97fa117c48a58bee3941e5e8b4393873501afe14
build time: 2026-02-04T20:26:22Z
built with: go1.25.5 linux/amd64
```

Host: Debian 13, kernel 6.12.63, single-node deploy (~250 nodes connected, mix of Windows/Linux Tailscale clients), TLS direct on :50443, sqlite DB.

## Trigger

A systemd service restart fired during `certbot renew --deploy-hook` (Let's Encrypt DNS-01 cert reload). The graceful shutdown of the old process and reconnect storm from the existing fleet (~250 nodes) collided with the new process's startup.

Timeline (local time, EDT):

```
11:22:41  old pid 1308 begins graceful shutdown ("Headscale stopped")
11:22:41  systemd starts new pid 359648
11:22:42  v0.28.0 startup: DB open, DERP region up, STUN up, listening on :50443
11:22:43  some "user msg: node not found code=404" errors
11:22:44  fleet begins reconnecting (~250 nodes)
11:22:47  PANIC — nil pointer deref in goroutine 159
11:22:47  systemd: "Main process exited, code=exited, status=2/INVALIDARGUMENT"
11:22:52  systemd: Scheduled restart job (counter=1)
11:22:53  new process starts clean, no recurrence since
```

## Stack trace

```
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
[signal SIGSEGV: segmentation violation code=0x1 addr=0x0 pc=0x137e83b]

goroutine 159 [running]:
github.com/juanfont/headscale/hscontrol/state.(*State).ListPeers(0x0?, 0x0?, {0x0, 0x1, 0xc001a0b860?})
	/home/runner/work/headscale/headscale/hscontrol/state/state.go:611 +0xfb
github.com/juanfont/headscale/hscontrol/mapper.(*mapper).buildFromChange(0xc0004b6cc0, 0xe8, 0x83, 0x0?)
	/home/runner/work/headscale/headscale/hscontrol/mapper/mapper.go:291 +0x368
github.com/juanfont/headscale/hscontrol/mapper.generateMapResponse({0x2451ea0, 0xc002a0f220}, 0xc0004b6cc0, {{0x20967bb, 0xb}, 0x0, 0x0, 0x0, 0x0, 0x0, ...})
	/home/runner/work/headscale/headscale/hscontrol/mapper/batcher.go:125 +0x315
github.com/juanfont/headscale/hscontrol/mapper.handleNodeChange({0x2451ea0, 0xc002a0f220}, 0xc0004b6cc0, {{0x20967bb, 0xb}, 0x0, 0x0, 0x0, 0x0, 0x0, ...})
	/home/runner/work/headscale/headscale/hscontrol/mapper/batcher.go:145 +0x112
github.com/juanfont/headscale/hscontrol/mapper.(*multiChannelNodeConn).change(...)
	/home/runner/work/headscale/headscale/hscontrol/mapper/batcher_lockfree.go:765
github.com/juanfont/headscale/hscontrol/mapper.(*LockFreeBatcher).worker(0xc0009b4980, 0xf)
	/home/runner/work/headscale/headscale/hscontrol/mapper/batcher_lockfree.go:257 +0x4c5
created by github.com/juanfont/headscale/hscontrol/mapper.(*LockFreeBatcher).doWork in goroutine 131
	/home/runner/work/headscale/headscale/hscontrol/mapper/batcher_lockfree.go:176 +0x58
```

## Analysis

The receiver of `ListPeers` is nil (`0x0?`). The call site at `mapper.go:291` is `peers := m.state.ListPeers(nodeID, resp.PeersChanged...)` — so `m.state` (the mapper's `State` reference) is nil when the worker fires.

`LockFreeBatcher.doWork()` at `batcher_lockfree.go:176` spawns its worker pool with `go b.worker(i + 1)`. A worker (goroutine 159) picked up a queued change event for an inbound `multiChannelNodeConn` and ran the full mapper path before `mapper.state` had a non-nil value. The connect storm of ~250 simultaneous reconnections makes this race much more likely to fire on production startup than in unit tests.

## Recovery

systemd's `Restart=on-failure` kicked in after 5s. The second cold start ran clean (no parallel cert-renew event, slightly staggered reconnects), and the panic has not recurred. No data loss; no operator action required.

## Related

#3125 already tracks `LockFreeBatcher` as race-prone — but the listed failure mode there (`TestBatcherScalabilityAllToAll` panics with "send on closed channel" during shutdown) is a different exit path than this *startup* nil-state race. Filing as a separate issue since the production stack trace is concrete and may help triage.

I'm happy to capture additional journal context or test a candidate fix if useful.

title: [Feature] Option to replace or limit stored policies
body:
### Use case

Hi,

When updating ACL policies via the gRPC policy API, Headscale currently inserts a new row into the policies table on every update and keeps all previous policies indefinitely.

In setups where policies are updated frequently, this leads to unbounded growth of the policies table.
In our case (SQLite backend), the database grew to ~900 MB, almost entirely due to historical policy rows, and required manual cleanup + restart to recover disk space.

This seems expected behavior today, but it’s problematic operationally, especially for SQLite where disk space cannot be reclaimed online.

### Description

Would it be possible to add an explicit, opt‑in way to avoid unbounded policy growth? 

For example:
- a “replace policy” / “set policy (overwrite)” API
- or a config option to keep only the latest N policies
- or an explicit policy‑pruning operation

The current append‑only behavior could remain the default; the request is for an optional mechanism for users who don’t need full policy history.

title: integration: harden suite against Docker Hub 429s and timing flakes
body:
Two flake causes. Docker Hub anonymous pulls hit the 100/6h per-IP cap on shared CI. `tsic.Curl` returned `("", nil)` on empty bodies, hiding failures from `EventuallyWithT`.

Adds `docker/login-action` on every job that pulls, with a guard so fork PRs skip it. `tsic.Curl` errors on empty bodies; `tsic.Traceroute` gains `-w 1 -q 1`. libnetwork settle-waits sit inside the Disconnect/Reconnect primitives so HA tests stop racing bridge reprogramming. Shared timeout/retry constants replace 295 ad-hoc literals.

Two control-plane fixes for related flakes. MagicDNS root-domain `Routes` ship as empty non-nil slices rather than `nil`, since `dns.Config.Clone` in wgengine drops nil-valued map entries and a major `LinkChange` reapplies the cloned config — wiping `/etc/resolv.conf` until the next route-changing netmap. HA prober batches probe results per cycle through a single `BatchSetNodeUnhealthy` and defers a cycle when any probe is fresh-session or reconnected mid-probe; the election fallback no longer picks `candidates[0]` when the previous primary has gone, so simultaneous dual-disconnect cannot flap primary onto an unreachable node.

HA election now has a property-test in `hscontrol/state/primaries_property_test.go` (rapid, 2000 checks), a servertest-level property-test gated by `util.IsCI()` for long local sweeps, and an invariant catalogue at `hscontrol/state/HA_INVARIANTS.md`.

title: [Bug] via grant does not match subnet router when destination is a broader prefix than the advertised route
body:
### Is this a support request?

- [x] This is not a support request

### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Current Behavior

Headscale Policy:
```yaml
{
  "tagOwners": {
    "tag:subnet-router": ["exampleuser@"]
  },
  "hosts": {
    "example-4via6": "fd7a:115c:a1e0:b1a::/64"
  },
  "grants": [
    {
      "src": ["exampleuser@"],
      "dst": ["example-4via6"],
      "via": ["tag:subnet-router"],
      "ip": ["tcp:3389", "icmp:*"]
    }
  ]
}
```

The subnet router announces and has approved the subnet:
fd7a:115c:a1e0:b1a:0:13:ad2:7300/120

Client devices associated with the user `exampleuser` cannot ping devices within that subnet.

### Expected Behavior

Client devices associated with the user exampleuser should be able to ping devices in the range fd7a:115c:a1e0:b1a:0:13:ad2:7300/120

### Steps To Reproduce

- Build Headscale from the latest main branch.

- Create the following ACL file for Headscale:
```yaml
{
  "tagOwners": {
    "tag:subnet-router": ["exampleuser@"]
  },
  "hosts": {
    "example-4via6": "ffd7a:115c:a1e0:b1a::/64"
  },
  "grants": [
    {
      "src": ["exampleuser@"],
      "dst": ["example-4via6"],
      "via": ["tag:subnet-router"],
      "ip": ["tcp:3389", "icmp:*"]
    }
  ]
}
```
- Create the user exampleuser.

- Add a test node, advertise and approve the subnet:
fd7a:115c:a1e0:b1a:0:13:ad2:7300/120

- Add the tag subnet-router to the node.

Additionally, you have to add another grant for the node to become visible to the user’s node:

```yaml
{
  "src": ["exampleuser@"],
  "dst": ["tag:subnet-router"],
  "ip":  ["icmp:*"],
}
```
This should not be necessary, but I already saw some issues mentioning this. In my tests, the node was not visible to the source node without this grant, but this should not have anything to do with the issue

I think this issue comes down to exact prefix matching in the via path.

In `compileViaForNode()` and `ViaRoutesForPeer()`, Headscale appears to check whether the grant `dst` prefix is exactly contained in the subnet router's `SubnetRoutes()`:

```go
slices.Contains(nodeSubnetRoutes, dstPrefix)
```

This only works when the policy destination exactly matches the route advertised and approved by the subnet router.

If dst is a broader host alias or broader literal prefix, for example fd7a:115c:a1e0:b1a ::/64, and the router advertises a contained route such as fd7a:115c:a1e0:b1a:0:13:ad2:7300/120, the comparison fails even though the advertised route is inside the allowed destination prefix.

title: hscontrol: gate proxy header trust on trusted_proxies
body:
chi's `middleware.RealIP` was mounted unconditionally, so any client could send `X-Real-IP: 1.2.3.4` or `X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4` and have the spoofed value land in `r.RemoteAddr` and the access-log `remote=` field. Benign in-tree today but breaks fail2ban-style log scraping and any future code that keys off the source IP.

New top-level `trusted_proxies` config option (list of CIDRs). Empty (the default) skips the middleware entirely. Non-empty mounts a gated middleware that honours `True-Client-IP` / `X-Real-IP` / `X-Forwarded-For` only when `r.RemoteAddr` is inside one of the configured prefixes, and strips those three headers from every request whose peer is not trusted. `X-Forwarded-For` is parsed via `realclientip-go`'s rightmost-trusted-range strategy so a prepended value cannot win in a proxy chain.

Behavioural change for operators behind a reverse proxy: they now need to set `trusted_proxies` to the proxy's source CIDR to keep seeing the real client IP in `remote=`. Documented in `docs/ref/integration/reverse-proxy.md`.

title: policy/v2: match via-grant destinations by prefix overlap
body:
`compileViaForNode` (`hscontrol/policy/v2/compiled.go:686`) and `ViaRoutesForPeer` (`hscontrol/policy/v2/policy.go:998, 1089`) used `slices.Contains(subnetRoutes, dstPrefix)` to decide whether a node advertised a grant destination. Equality rejects any non-identical prefix pair, so a via grant with broader or narrower `dst` than the advertised subnet emitted no filter rule and added no route to the viewer's `AllowedIPs`. Tailscale SaaS uses containment in either direction.

Switch the filter-rule path to `slices.ContainsFunc(routes, dst.Overlaps)` and keep the literal `dst` in `DstPorts`. Append overlapping advertised routes to `ViaRoutesForPeer.Include` / `Exclude` rather than the dst. Rewrite the multi-router HA election and regular-grant overlap to key off the matched routes. Resolve `*Host` aliases to `*Prefix` once in `compileOneViaGrant` and at the top of `ViaRoutesForPeer` so the type switch reaches them.

Five new `testdata/grant_results/via-grant-v47..v51.hujson` lock the SaaS shape: broader literal dst, narrower literal dst, host-alias dst, disjoint dst (negative), and the reporter's exact 4via6 case. `TestGrantsCompat` replays them; existing v14-v46 captures stay green.

Fixes #3267

title: [Feature] Dynamic client node list reload for HA setups
body:
### Use case

Deploying a High-Availability (HA) Headscale setup in a Kubernetes cluster using multiple pods (one primary/leader and several secondary/replica pods) behind a load balancer (Envoy) to ensure seamless failover if a node or the primary pod goes down.

### Description

Currently, Headscale only reads the list of registered client nodes from the database at startup. While ACL rules can be reloaded dynamically, the client node cache is static.

Because of this, auxiliary/secondary pods remain unaware of any newly connected or registered clients during runtime. If traffic from a new client hits a secondary pod (or if a failover occurs), the connection is dropped with an "unknown node" error. To make the secondary pods aware of the new clients, a full restart of the pods is required, which defeats the purpose of an HA setup.

### Contribution

- [ ] I can write the design doc for this feature
- [ ] I can contribute this feature

### How can it be implemented?

Dynamic Cache Refresh (Hot-reload): Implement a mechanism to reload or refresh the client node list from the database dynamically without requiring a full application restart, similar to how ACL rules are currently reloaded.

Event-driven Updates / Polling: Headscale could either periodically poll the database for new nodes or trigger a cache refresh event whenever a new client successfully registers or updates its state.

API Endpoint / Signal: Alternatively, introduce an administrative API endpoint or a specific signal (like SIGHUP) that external tools or Kubernetes lifecycles can trigger to force a configuration and node list reload.

title: integration: pre-pull released tailscale images for fork-PR CI
body:
Fork PRs without `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` anonymous-pull `tailscale/tailscale:vX.Y` at test time and hit Docker Hub rate limits, causing flakes across the ~56 integration test jobs.

A new `build-tailscale-released` job pulls `MustTestVersions` from `ghcr.io/tailscale/tailscale` once per CI run and ships them to every test job as a gzipped tarball artifact, matching the shape of the existing headscale/HEAD/postgres caches. `integration/tsic/tsic.go` now references `ghcr.io/tailscale/tailscale`, so the `dockertestutil.PullWithAuth` `InspectImage` short-circuit picks up the loaded image and skips the network entirely.

Version list is driven by a new `hi list-versions` subcommand that reads `hscontrol/capver`. Single source of truth, no YAML duplication: adding a version in capver propagates to CI on the next run.

ghcr.io public reads need no auth, so the new job has no docker login step.

title: db: detect Go pseudo-versions as dev in upgrade-path check
body:
Upgrading from an untagged `main-sha` docker tag to `v0.29.0-beta.1` failed with:

```
headscale version v0.29.0-beta.1 cannot be used with a database last used by v0.0.0-20260520093041-e4e742c776ee, upgrading more than one minor version at a time is not supported
```

`runtime/debug.BuildInfo` returns a Go module pseudo-version (`vX.Y.Z-<timestamp>-<hash>`) for untagged builds. `isDev` in `hscontrol/db/versioncheck.go` only filtered `""`, `"dev"`, `"(devel)"`, so the pseudo-version slipped through and `parseVersion` coerced it to semver `{0,0,0}` by stripping after the first `-`. The pseudo-version was then written to `database_versions` and the next real release tripped the multi-minor guard at `versioncheck.go:228`.

Two symptoms of the same bug: a fresh `main-sha` run poisons the database and blocks the next release; a `main-sha` run against an already-versioned database is rejected as a downgrade.

`pseudoVersionTime` parses the trailing `<sep><14 digits>-<12 hex>` suffix with `regexp` + `time.Parse`, covering all three Go pseudo-version forms (`v0.0.0-…`, `vX.Y.Z-pre.0.…`, `vX.Y.(Z+1)-0.…`). `isDev` delegates to it after the existing literal checks. The dev gate at `db.go:790` already prevents pseudo-versions from being written, so already-poisoned databases self-heal on the next real-release start.

Fixes #3281

title: [Feature] HTTP/2 fallback for TS2021 handshake to support Cloudflare Tunnel and restrictive proxies
body: ### Use case Cloudflare Tunnel is extremely common in homelab setups — it allows exposing services without opening firewall ports or exposing a home IP address. Many self-hosters want to run Headscale behind it for exactly this reason. Currently external node registration is impossible through Cloudflare Tunnel because the TS2021 control channel handshake fails. The practical impact is that nodes must be registered on LAN, making remote onboarding of new devices (e.g. a TAKServer deployment for worldwide field access) impossible without exposing infrastructure or paying for a VPS. Related closed issues: #1468, #2379 ### Description The TS2021 Noise handshake uses: POST /ts2021 HTTP/1.1 Connection: Upgrade Upgrade: tailscale-control-protocol Cloudflare Tunnel only passes `Upgrade` headers on HTTP GET requests (per RFC 6455). On POST requests, cloudflared strips the `Upgrade` header entirely (confirmed bug: cloudflare/cloudflared#883, open since 2023, still unfixed). Headscale then correctly rejects the stripped request: WRN No Upgrade header in TS2021 request. If headscale is behind a reverse proxy, make sure it is configured to pass WebSockets through. What partially works: HTTP long-poll fallback keeps already-registered nodes connected, but initial external registration fails with 500 Internal Server Error. What I have tried: - Custom Traefik middleware passing all Upgrade header values → works on LAN ✅ - Cloudflare Tunnel HTTP mode direct to Headscale → Upgrade header stripped on POST ❌ - Cloudflare Tunnel HTTP mode via Traefik → same result, Upgrade stripped before Traefik ❌ - Cloudflare Tunnel TCP mode → requires `cloudflared access` on client side, not possible with standard Tailscale clients ❌ - cloudflared `http2OriginMode: true` + `protocol: http2` → still strips Upgrade header on POST ❌ External references: - cloudflare/cloudflared#883 — confirmed bug, Upgrade stripped on POST - cloudflare/cloudflared#990 — feature request, general Upgrade support - traefik/traefik#12609 — Traefik custom Upgrade header support request Environment: - Headscale v0.28.0 - cloudflared 2025.1.0 - Traefik v3 - Docker on Ubuntu/ Server homelab - Tailscale clients: Android (S21+), Windows 11 ### Contribution - [ ] I can write the design doc for this feature - [ ] I can contribute this feature ### How can it be implemented? HTTP/2 natively supports full-duplex bidirectional streams without requiring the HTTP Upgrade mechanism at all. If Headscale detects that `/ts2021` was called via POST but the `Upgrade: tailscale-control-protocol` header is absent (stripped by an intermediate proxy), instead of immediately returning 426 Upgrade Required it could attempt to establish the Noise channel over a plain HTTP/2 stream. The Noise protocol payload is transport-agnostic — it does not care whether the underlying transport used the Upgrade mechanism or a native HTTP/2 stream. The client already negotiates HTTP/2 where available. This would require no changes to the Tailscale client and no special proxy configuration from the user. Proxies that strip the Upgrade header would transparently fall through to the HTTP/2 stream path.

title: policy: key autogroup:self invalidation on UserID not User view
body:
A node restarting `tailscaled` on a tailnet with an `autogroup:self` policy crashed the control server: every `/machine/map` returned 500, so no node could fetch a map.

`invalidateAutogroupSelfCache` bucketed nodes by `node.User().ID()`, dereferencing the `User` association view. The `NodeStore` holds nodes by value with `User` as a `*User` that only some write paths hydrate, so a non-tagged node could reach `SetNodes` with `UserID` set but `User` nil — `UserView.ID()` then dereferenced a nil pointer and panicked. `autogroup:self` and this per-node invalidation path are new in 0.29, so the regression only surfaced this cycle.

Bucket by `node.TypedUserID()` instead, reading the `UserID` field directly. `UserID` is the authoritative ownership field for non-tagged nodes, so invalidation no longer depends on a hydrated association and every `.User().ID()` site in the function is fixed at once.

Other `.User().ID()` call sites on the filter-compilation path share the same latent assumption but are fed by a preloaded snapshot and not exercised by this crash; hardening those is a separate follow-up.

```bash
# OK
```

But after we enable  **exitnode** as the exit node:
```
clientnode$ tailscale up --exit-node=exitnode --accept-routes --login-server=https://vpn.example.com
```

pinging `88.88.88.3` is not working anymore:
```bash
clientnode$ ping -c1 88.88.88.3
# FAIL

clientnode$ ping -c1 8.8.8.8
# Still OK
```

The problem appears only for destinations that belong to the external subnet directly connected to the exit node itself, in this example: `88.88.88.0/24`.



### Expected Behavior

When **clientnode** uses **exitnode** as an exit node, it should be able to reach any publicly routable Internet address through that exit node, including addresses from the external subnet directly connected to **exitnode**.

In this example, ping from **clientnode** to both `8.8.8.8` and `88.88.88.3` should work.

Note: we do not want **exitnode** to announce `88.88.88.0/24` as a subnet route to all clients. Clients that do not use **exitnode** as an exit node should continue reaching `88.88.88.3` through their normal Internet route, with their own public source IP address visible on the Internet.

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Connect to two nodes to a Headscale/Tailscale network:

   - **exitnode**
     - advertises itself as an exit node (and is allowed to be used as exitnode in ACL)
     - has an external interface with IP `88.88.88.2/24`
     - the directly connected external subnet is `88.88.88.0/24`

   - **clientnode**
     - uses **exitnode** as its exit node

2. From **clientnode**, verify that both public IP addresses are reachable before enabling the exit node:

```bash
   ping -c1 88.88.88.3
   ping -c1 8.8.8.8
````
Both pings should succeed.

3. Enable **exitnode** as the exit node on **clientnode**:

```bash
   tailscale up \
     --exit-node=exitnode \
     --accept-routes \
     --login-server=https://vpn.example.com
```

4. From **clientnode**, ping a normal Internet address:

```bash
   ping -c1 8.8.8.8
```

This still works.

5. From **clientnode**, ping another public IP address from the external subnet directly connected to **exitnode**:

```bash
   ping -c1 88.88.88.3
```

Observe that the ping to `88.88.88.3` fails, even though general Internet access through the exit node still works.

### Environment

```markdown
- OS: Gentoo Linux
- Headscale version: headscale version v0.27.2-rc.1+dirty
  commit: c6d399a66ca9ec94bb84e78e8edf9a31981f554c
- Tailscale version: 1.96.5
```

### Runtime environment

- [ ] Headscale is behind a (reverse) proxy
- [x] Headscale runs in a container

### Debug information

We found a workaround: advertise `88.88.88.0/24` on **exitnode**, but do not approve this route in Headscale. 
This prevents the route from being distributed to clients, but it makes the local `tailscaled` on **exitnode** allow traffic from **clientnode** to destinations inside `88.88.88.0/24`.

Still, this feels more like a workaround than a proper fix.

The current logic seems intended to exclude LAN/private networks from automatic exit-node access. But in this case the excluded subnet is a publicly routable Internet subnet directly connected to the exit node, not a private LAN.

Maybe publicly routable directly connected networks should not be treated the same way as LAN/private networks when shrinking the default route for an exit node.

title: [Bug] 0.29 beta triggers PolicyChange on every reconnect causing CPU spikes
body: ### Is this a support request? - [x] This is not a support request ### Is there an existing issue for this? - [x] I have searched the existing issues ### Current Behavior Note: this issue was prepared and created by an AI coding agent using operator-provided production observations and local source-code investigation. After upgrading from `v0.28.0` to `v0.29.0-beta.1`, headscale CPU usage started spiking to 100% when existing nodes reconnected. The spike correlated with the `poll.go` log line `node has connected`. The same unconditional reconnect behavior is present in `v0.29.0-beta.2`. The likely regression is commit `380f5313`: `state: trigger PolicyChange on every Connect and Disconnect` That change appends `change.PolicyChange()` on every `State.Connect` and `State.Disconnect`. `PolicyChange` sets `RequiresRuntimePeerComputation`, so a normal reconnect can cause runtime policy/netmap recomputation for connected peers. On a small 1 vCore VM this saturated CPU. After deploying a local hotfix that avoids `PolicyChange` for ordinary reconnects/disconnects, the CPU spikes disappeared. A 7-day CPU graph showed frequent sharp spikes before the hotfix and a much lower/stable CPU profile after deployment. ### Expected Behavior A normal reconnect of an already-registered node should send lightweight online/offline peer updates, not a full runtime policy recomputation, unless policy-sensitive state actually changed. `PolicyChange` should still be emitted for cases that need it, such as: - primary route ownership changes - policy/user/tag/node identity changes - liveness-sensitive policy features such as `via` or `tailscale.com/cap/relay` ### Steps To Reproduce 1. Run headscale `v0.28.0`. 2. Upgrade to `v0.29.0-beta.1` or `v0.29.0-beta.2`. 3. Use a small VM, e.g. 1 vCore. 4. Let existing nodes reconnect, or restart headscale so clients reconnect. 5. Observe CPU spike around the `node has connected` log line. 6. Apply a local hotfix that gates reconnect/disconnect `PolicyChange`. 7. Observe that the CPU spikes disappear. ### Environment - OS: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, noble - Kernel: `6.8.0-117-generic` - Headscale version: reproduced after upgrade from `v0.28.0` to `v0.29.0-beta.1`; code path still present in `v0.29.0-beta.2` - Tailscale version: reproduced with different Tailscale client versions, including: ```text 1.98.3 tailscale commit: a16e0f20cff0acd5617fd1b315df32cdad17a8fa long version: 1.98.3-ta16e0f20c-ge0c644472 other commit: e0c6444725a27ff911a18cc4b18575d8700339d5 go version: go1.26.3 (tailscale/go e877d97384) ``` - CPU: 1 vCore VM - Database: SQLite - Policy mode: file - `tuning.batcher_workers`: not configured, so default was used ### Runtime environment - [ ] Headscale is behind a (reverse) proxy - [ ] Headscale runs in a container Headscale is not behind a reverse proxy and is not running in a container. ### Debug information Attached CPU graph: 7-day headscale CPU usage. The high spikes occurred before the local hotfix; the arrow marks the period after deploying the fix, where CPU spikes disappeared. Important code path: - `hscontrol/poll.go` calls `State.Connect` - `State.Connect` logs `node connected` - `poll.go` logs `node has connected` - returned changes are passed to `Headscale.Change` - `change.PolicyChange()` causes mapper runtime peer computation for connected nodes In `v0.29.0-beta.2`, the relevant behavior is: ```go // State.Connect c = append(c, change.PolicyChange()) // State.Disconnect cs := []change.Change{change.NodeOfflineFor(node), c, change.PolicyChange()} ``` The local hotfix that resolved the production CPU spike changed this behavior to only emit `PolicyChange` on connect/disconnect when policy liveness actually affects generated netmaps, e.g. `via` or `cap/relay`, or when route-primary state changes. Focused tests added locally: - ordinary node connect does not emit runtime `PolicyChange` - ordinary node disconnect does not emit runtime `PolicyChange` - liveness-sensitive policy still emits `PolicyChange` - `via` and `cap/relay` policies are classified as liveness-sensitive Verification after deploying the hotfix: CPU spikes are gone. The 7-day CPU graph confirms the change from repeated sharp spikes to a lower/stable CPU profile after the fix.
